note.note: According to dates and times stamped on this telegram, it was sent by JJ (“Foike”) from Trieste on 26 May 1920 at “23.25,” or 11:25 p.m. It was received in Sirmione on 27 May at “8.50” (a.m.).
note.p: “I leave Monday morning, barring incidents [or accidents].” In a letter to his father, Pound translated the phrase “salvo incidenti” as “if the bloody trains run” (Ezra Pound to his Parents: Letters 1885-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 468). The Monday following 26 May (the date of this telegram) was 31 May. JJ both cabled and wrote Pound on 31 May (Ellmann misdates the letter as 5 June) to say that he had been prevented from leaving Trieste by the wreck of a passenger train on the line and by cancellations resulting from a railway strike. Now he hoped to meet Pound in England, en route for Ireland, in the near future, as his present plan was to get out of Trieste for several months and finish Ulysses in Dublin or Galway in the relative peace of his nuclear family (Pound/Joyce 167-69; LII 467-69). Pound wrote JJ on 2 June that he and Dorothy in Sirmione had “waited dinner till 8:00 and I had prepared such a nice opening speech” (Pound/Joyce 170). His heart was set on meeting up with JJ in this northern Italian paradise; with his usual eccentric efficiency, he wrote long letters suggesting ideas that might bring JJ to Sirmione despite the setbacks (Pound/Joyce 170-77). Forrest Read nicely refers to Pound in these busy days as “Catullus’s one-man chamber of commerce” (Pound/Joyce 175).

JJ apparently started for Sirmione, then turned back. Pound himself nearly left for Trieste, then thought better of it and resigned himself to meeting JJ in Paris sometime later. Then, on the night of 8 June, as if stepping from one of the thunderclouds that had been threatening for days, JJ arrived by train at Desenzano, near Sirmione, “bringing,” he later wrote, “my son with me to act as a lightning conductor” (LI 142). Pound met them and took them to Sirmione, where they spent two days. JJ thought Pound “a large bundle of unpredictable electricity” and “a miracle of ebulliency, gusto, and help” (Pound/Joyce 178). Pound found JJ “pleasing; after the first shell of cantankerous Irishman, I got the impression that the real man is the author of Chamber Music. The sensitive: the rest is the genius; the registration of realities on the … delicate temperament of the early poems” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 189).

The flaps and borders of this telegram are filled on both sides with notes scrawled in pencil by Pound. It is uncertain where, when, or whether he made use of these jottings, but various Poundian themes emerge clearly. We find in these jottings (see photographic images) Pound’s deep interest in the musical values of verse, its “beat” and “pitch.” The surges of Greek quantitative meter he believed he could hear surviving in the verse of the English poet and composer Thomas Campion (1567–1620). In 1920, Pound still set his poetic compass by the progress he had made, from his early rhyming experiments of 1909, to the Imagism of 1912-1914 and the Vorticism of 1914. This history of poetic development is glanced at in Pound’s notations: “1 rhym c. 1909. / 2 imag (des[?]) / 2 vort.”

Some of the penciled themes are echoed in Pound’s article, “The Island of Paris: A Letter,” The Dial, vol. 69, no. 6 (December 1920), where he observed: “The visual art in poetry reached its zenith with Li Po; onomatopoeia and rhythmic art are perhaps at their best … in parts of Homer, Bion, and Sappho …. As one goes to the Provençal, and to Arnaut [Daniel] in particular for a sort of contrapunto of line-terminations, rhyme in its most developed arrangements” (636). This association of visual, imagistic qualities with Chinese poetry, rhythms and cadences with Greek poetry, and line-end sound experiments with Provençal verse can be glimpsed in Pound’s jottings. And the key to the mysterious little pie-chart that Pound drew and glossed as “arab,” is found in the same article: “And musical notation? … people have tried various devices from our very unsatisfactory own, to the circular bars of the Arabs, divided, like unjust mince-pies, from centre to circumference” (638).

Pound’s work with magazines – The Little Review, The Egoist, and The New Age – was much on his mind in 1920, as his association with the New York journal The Dial was growing stronger; he set down a brief memorandum of his editorial associations: “pub. proc. L.R. N.A. no Eg.” His tendency to define aesthetic values by pointing to negative embodiments is also present in his jotted references to the British classicist Gilbert Murray (1866-1957), whose verse translations of Greek drama Pound and T.S. Eliot detested, and to the English novelist Arnold Bennett (1867-1931), whom Pound classed with other realist authors of the day as dabblers in “hyper aesthesia,” an art of verbal excess lacking the qualities of definite form and incisive thought. In the notation “R.A. superfic,” there may even be a glance at the English poet, critic, and novelist Richard Aldington (1892-1962), whose articles in the Times Literary Supplement and other periodicals Pound sometimes found superficial.

Pound’s famous contempt for universities – or “beaneries” – is also evident in these jottings (“mod. univ.”). He had special reason to be irritated with higher learning just now; he and his father were attempting to persuade the University of Pennsylvania – that “gehenna” – to award him the Ph.D. on the basis of course work he had done years earlier for his M.A. there and his record of publication since. The faculty red-taped the matter and denied the eccentric, expatriate Pound a doctorate, leading him to reflect that he had at least sampled “the psychology of the University / / scientifically valuable as a record of the Spirit of the Age” (Ezra Pound to his Parents: Letters, 466). Pound’s jottings may also express his frustration with organized religion (“rel. builds nothing”), which he described in 1919 as “an attempt to enforce a type or a cliché; an attempt to impose a thought-mould [sic] upon others” (“Pastiche. The Regional. I.,” The New Age, vol. 25, no. 7 [12 June 1919]: 124).
